chapter.title: Stations and the belt

cards.body: Why does every n8n screenshot look like boxes on a wire? Because that is the whole trick. Each box is a *node*, one station on the assembly line that does exactly one job: fetch, change, send. What slides along the wire is an *item*, a small parcel with named fields inside, like name, email, amount. **Each station does one job and hands its parcels to the next.**
cards.simpler: Every n8n picture looks like boxes joined by a wire. That is the whole idea. Each box is a node. A node is one station on a line, and it does one job: fetch something, change something, or send something. What moves along the wire is an item. An item is a small parcel with named fields inside, like name, email, amount. **Each station does one job and hands its parcels to the next.**

cards.prompt: Your line is Schedule Trigger, then a Weather node, then a Slack node. At 7am Slack posts 'Rain at 3pm, bring a coat'. Where did the Slack station get those words?

options.text: It checked the weather itself, since it needed the words.
From the parcel the Weather station handed down the belt.
From the Schedule Trigger, which knows the time and the forecast.

whyNot.a: That's the Weather station's job, not Slack's: one station, one job, and Slack only sends.
whyNot.c: That's the bell, not the belt: the trigger wakes the line up and carries little more than the time.

cards.reteach: A node never reaches past its own job. Slack sends; it does not fetch. Whatever it sends arrived as an item from the node before it, which got it from the node before that.

cards.title: One station, one job
cards.body:
A node is one box on the canvas. You add one with the plus button, pick what it does, and it does only that. Fetch a forecast. Add a row. Send a message. Nothing more.

Think of a sandwich counter with three people: one spreads, one fills, one wraps. Nobody does two steps. That is why a working line is often 3 boring nodes, not 1 clever one.

You'd think a smarter box is better. It's the reverse. **Small nodes are easy to test and easy to swap**, and when one breaks you know exactly which one.
cards.simpler:
A node is one box on the screen. You add it with the plus button and pick its job. It does only that job. Fetch a forecast. Add a row. Send a message.

Picture a sandwich counter with three people. One spreads, one fills, one wraps. Nobody does two steps. A working line is often three plain nodes, not one clever one.

**Small nodes are easy to test and easy to swap**, and when one breaks you know which one.

cards.title: 30 parcels, 30 messages
cards.body: Dev builds a line: Schedule Trigger, then a node that reads his signup sheet, then Slack. He opens the sheet node and presses the test button. The output panel says *30 items*: one parcel per row, each with the same fields, name and plan. He connects Slack and runs the whole line. His team channel gets 30 'New signup!' posts in 4 seconds. Nothing was broken. **Most nodes run once per item**, so 30 parcels in means 30 messages out.
cards.simpler: Dev builds a line. A Schedule Trigger, then a node that reads his signup sheet, then Slack. He opens the sheet node and presses test. The output panel says 30 items. That is one parcel per row, all with the same fields, name and plan. He connects Slack and runs the line. His team channel gets 30 'New signup!' posts in 4 seconds. Nothing broke. **Most nodes run once per item**, so 30 parcels in means 30 messages out.

cards.prompt: Maya's line: a trigger, then the Customer Datastore training node, which hands out 5 sample customers, then a Send Email node. She runs it. How many emails go out?

options.text: 1, because the email node is one station.
5, one per item on the belt.
0, until she adds a loop node to go through the customers.

whyNot.a: That's counting stations, not parcels: one station runs once for every item that reaches it.
whyNot.c: That's a habit from other tools, not n8n: it walks each item down the belt on its own, no loop needed.

cards.reteach: Picture 5 parcels arriving at the wrapping station. The wrapper does not wrap once and stop. It wraps all 5, one at a time, with the same motion. An n8n node does the same with items.

cards.title: Reading the belt
cards.body:
To see what a station hands on, open it and press the test button. The panel on the left shows what came in. The panel on the right shows what goes out. At the top of the output sits the count: *1 item*, *5 items*, or the quiet alarm, *0 items*.

Think of a customs desk that opens every parcel. The Table view lays items out as rows, one row per item, one column per field. The JSON view shows the same parcel as raw text with braces. Same data, two windows.

**The output panel is the only honest witness.** Not the wire, not your memory of what the node should do.
cards.simpler:
Open a station and press the test button. The left panel shows what came in. The right panel shows what goes out. At the top sits the count: 1 item, 5 items, or the quiet alarm, 0 items.

Table view lays items out as rows, one per item. JSON view shows the same parcel as raw text with braces.

**The output panel is the only honest witness.** Not the wire, not your memory of what the node should do.

cards.body:
Jonah builds 5 nodes in a row, presses run on the whole line, and gets a blank Slack message. He spends 40 minutes staring at the Slack node. The Slack node was fine. Node 2 was handing on 0 items, so everything after it had nothing to send.

Spot it: test one station at a time, and **read the count before you add the next box**.
cards.simpler:
Jonah builds 5 nodes in a row, runs the whole line, and gets a blank Slack message. He spends 40 minutes staring at the Slack node. The Slack node was fine. Node 2 was handing on 0 items, so everything after it had nothing to send. Think of a shut valve halfway along a water pipe.

Spot it: test one station at a time, and **read the count before you add the next box**.

cards.prompt: You open the second node in your line and its output panel reads '0 items'. What does that mean for the third node?

options.text: It runs anyway with empty fields, so you'll get blank messages.
It has no parcels to work on, so it does nothing.
It asks the trigger to run again and fetch more.

whyNot.a: That's a parcel with empty fields, not no parcel: 0 items means the belt is bare, so nothing reaches the next station.
whyNot.c: That's wishful thinking, not the belt: items only move forward, and no station can ring the bell.

cards.reteach: Items are the only thing that moves down the belt. A node with 0 items out gives the next node nothing to run on, so the line goes quiet from that point. Find out why the parcel count dropped to 0 there.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Each node is one station that does one job, and the data between them travels as items, small parcels with named fields. Open any node, press test, and **the output panel tells you exactly how many parcels it hands on** and what is inside each.

Tomorrow: the 2-minute permission slip that lets n8n act as you in Gmail or Slack.
cards.simpler:
Each node is one station that does one job. The data between stations travels as items, which are small parcels with named fields inside. Open any node and press test. **The output panel tells you exactly how many parcels it hands on** and what is inside each one.

Tomorrow: the 2-minute permission slip that lets n8n act as you in Gmail or Slack.

cards.body: In n8n, add the Customer Datastore (n8n training) node after any trigger, pick the option that returns all people, press the test button, and read the item count. Then flip Table to JSON and find the same field in both.
cards.simpler: In n8n, add the Customer Datastore (n8n training) node right after any trigger. Pick the option that returns all people. Press the test button and **read the item count** at the top of the output. Then switch the view from Table to JSON and find the same field in both. That proves the two views show the same parcel.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now connect three nodes in a row and read exactly what each station hands to the next.
